Scarlet Nexus is a surprisingly large game with varying quality. The game shares a lot of similarities with other “anime” RPG’s of the past few years, notably Tales of Arise and Astral Chain. I 100% completed the game, both Yuito and Kasane’s stories and all achievements, and I think only part of the game is worth your time.

There are 12 “Phases”, and Yuito and Kasane have their own stories for the first 9 Phases of Scarlet Nexus. Yuito’s story is the stronger of the two, with more satisfying combat, a more cohesive story, and access to better abilities. When your party comes back together in Chapter 10, Scarlet Nexus’ gameplay begins to shine. With the full kit at your disposal, the gameplay is extremely engaging and satisfying, the chemistry between characters picks up, and the story finally focuses on the main conflict. Chapter 10 and 12 are also the longest and most gameplay heavy, giving you plenty of time to enjoy the fully-powered gameplay. Up until this point, you get interrupted frequently with cutscenes, never letting you settle into the combat. I was ready to “Not Recommend” this game when I finished Chapter 8, but the final chapters changed my mind.The final chapter also includes some stellar boss fights that make the most of these mechanics, music, and characters. 

Unless you really enjoyed your first ~30 hour playthrough and are hungry for more, there’s very little reason to play through it again with the other protagonist. Kasane’s story has very little additional insights, and there is no secret ending that gets unlocked when you finish both. There are some additional combat encounters, achievements, a couple cool setpieces, and a bit more character development, but it took an additional 20 hours and barely felt worth it. 

Throughout the game, you’ll have chances to play “Bond Episodes” with your companions. These are meant to be played as they become available, as they tie into the story, but can be skipped if you don’t care for the supporting cast. I enjoyed them, and thought each character had great development, if a bit trope-y. They did tend to come in waves between Phases, leading to lengthy intermissions from the main story. Sometimes this didn’t make much sense and was disconnected from the sense of urgency present in the main scenario. I also disliked the “gift giving” you had to partake in, as it was mostly just navigating through menus and watching the same “thankyou” animation over and over. Each character has a culmination in their arc at the end, which was an unexpected but very welcome finishing touch. The story would have felt anti-climactic without them, as they're very much a part of it. 

The presentation is good, but not perfect. The music ranges from generic to “biopunk electro-swing”. The visual design, while a bit hard to see clearly in some busy encounters, is pulled off well. The “brain-punk” world design is interesting, and the monster design was good, but not varied enough. The cutscenes are about 80% comic style stills with voice acting ontop. I would have liked to see more done with the concept, but it’s kept fairly basic throughout. The other 20% are very smooth 3D animated cutscenes. The english voices were passable (with a couple remarkable performances by Karen and Arashi), and the translation didn’t have any glaring issues, just a few inaccurate subtitles. On my rig (GTX970 i5-4670k), performance was an issue at first and it took some time digging into settings to get the video to stop stuttering (1440p60fps) and to get the audio balance right (SFX were way too loud, preventing the music from being heard). There were some other technical issues, like the lock-on camera not behaving, and the minimap is rotation-locked, but the map menu cannot be. I appreciated the fact that dialogue during gameplay never got cut off or interrupted, so I could play at my own pace and didn’t have to stop and listen for fear of triggering an encounter up ahead. It's a thoughtful bit of level design I wish was more popular.

My only complaints from a gameplay standpoint are that it felt like the damage balance was off. Enemies hit way too hard, and the “armor” equipment barely did anything. The fights vs humans always felt unfair, with projectile attacks impossible to see coming. I would have welcomed the ability to interrupt long attack animations with a dodge, as the most powerful and visually satisfying attack combos always leave you open for attack. 

If you’re a fan of other flashy anime action games like Astral Chain and Tales Of, you’ll likely enjoy Scarlet Nexus. Unless you really fell in love with the world and characters, I wouldn’t recommend doing the second playthrough, as it doesn’t add anything substantial to the experience. Crank up the music and get in the flow of combat, but don't forget to take a breather now and again to catch up with your companions.

I first came across Scarlet Nexus years ago through a Gameranx video, and something about it quietly stayed with me ever since. At the time, I was not in a position to buy games freely, so I waited patiently until the Ultimate Edition finally reached a discounted price I felt comfortable with. Looking back now, I am genuinely glad I waited and experienced the complete package together.

What initially drew me toward the game were the combat animations, music, visual style, and cinematic finishers. There was a sense of freshness and personality in its presentation that felt different from many action games I had played over the years. More importantly, it felt like a game genuinely interested in trying its own ideas instead of simply following safer trends.

I started my first playthrough on Very Hard while still being relatively inexperienced with this style of action combat. Naturally, the beginning was rough. However, what first looked like flashy combat eventually revealed itself as a deeper system built around positioning, timing, movement, SAS combinations, and understanding enemy behavior properly. Scarlet Nexus unexpectedly pushed me into thinking far more strategically during fights than I originally anticipated.

Some of my most satisfying moments came from overcoming encounters and simulator challenges that initially felt impossible. At the same time, I also believe it is fair to acknowledge that the game occasionally struggles with vague descriptions, unclear optimization systems, and score requirements that can push combat closer toward stressful speedrunning rather than natural experimentation during certain S Rank challenges.

One gameplay issue that consistently frustrated me was the target lock on system. There were moments where I would naturally aim toward an enemy directly in front of me, only for the lock on to suddenly shift elsewhere instead. During simulator missions, this disrupted combat flow more than it should have. I adapted to it eventually, but it still felt like one of the weaker elements in an otherwise strong combat system.

Where Scarlet Nexus consistently succeeded for me was its combat presentation. The Brain Crush finishers, animation flow, visual effects, and overall battle rhythm gave encounters a stylish energy that remained satisfying long after the early excitement faded. The SAS system especially gave combat its own personality and kept battles evolving instead of becoming repetitive too quickly.

Visually, the futuristic art direction and battle presentation carried a distinctive atmosphere that helped Scarlet Nexus stand apart from many games I had experienced previously. Still, I had mixed feelings about the world design outside combat. Many environments felt strangely lifeless to me, almost like decorative set pieces rather than naturally lived in spaces.

Another aspect that weakened immersion for me was the panel based visual novel style cutscene presentation used throughout many dialogue sequences. I understand the artistic direction the developers were aiming for, but I personally would have preferred more immersive in engine cinematics during important emotional moments.

Story wise, Scarlet Nexus became far more interesting once the larger narrative finally began connecting together. I deliberately chose Kasane for my first route because I initially suspected she might be more deeply tied to the conflict itself, and the later revelations surrounding Karen Travers honestly surprised me once everything finally started making sense near the late game.

The more I reflected on Scarlet Nexus afterward, the more I realized the story quietly revolves around trauma, emotional attachment, regret, and the consequences of refusing to accept reality as it is. Karen completely changed how I viewed the overall narrative. In terms of sheer presence and conviction, he honestly reminded me somewhat of Megatron from the Transformers universe.

Interestingly, the more I progressed through the story, the more I realized I probably had more in common with Yuito Sumeragi than I initially expected. His personality traits involving quietly helping others, taking responsibility seriously, cooking, household chores, self improvement, and caring for people around him unexpectedly felt relatable to parts of my own life. What connected with me most was the way Yuito often helped people quietly without constantly seeking recognition for it, and how those same acts of kindness eventually returned back to him unexpectedly through the people around him.

The side missions were probably one of the weaker areas of the experience overall, although I still completed all of them because the rewards and progression benefits were useful while preparing for more difficult encounters later on. Replayability and achievement hunting eventually became one of the most mentally demanding parts of Scarlet Nexus for me. I completed both routes, cleared the major endgame content, replayed difficult encounters, and ultimately earned all 53 achievements. I mention that less as a flex and more as context for the perspective I developed while spending a significant amount of time with the game.

The simulator missions gradually became one of the more frustrating parts of the experience for me. While I understand the intention behind rewarding mastery and precision, some sections occasionally reduced the freedom and creativity of combat in favor of strict optimization. Repeated retries also created a constant sense of pressure that gradually reduced enjoyment during certain stretches of the endgame. Long sessions focused heavily on speed and precision eventually left noticeable strain on my hands and arms at times, which reminded me that games should still remain enjoyable at their core.

Despite all those criticisms, my respect for Scarlet Nexus itself never disappeared. Throughout the experience, the game consistently felt like a project filled with creativity, ambition, and individuality. Even when certain systems frustrated me, I could still clearly see the passion and experimentation behind the overall design philosophy.

The music and audio design also left generally positive impressions on me. The opening theme immediately created a strong atmosphere, while some calmer tracks throughout the game carried a peaceful and harmonious tone that I appreciated deeply. I also played entirely with the English voice acting, and overall I felt it suited the anime inspired tone fairly well.

After completing both routes, replaying difficult encounters, finishing the endgame content, and eventually earning every achievement, I can honestly say Scarlet Nexus became an experience I will likely remember for years to come. Not because it was perfect, but because underneath all its imperfections, there was still a sincerity and creative ambition that connected with me.

I would comfortably recommend Scarlet Nexus to players who enjoy stylish action combat, anime inspired storytelling, and gradually mastering layered gameplay systems over time. Personally, I believe the Ultimate Edition becomes the best way to experience the game once discounted properly, since it allows players to experience the complete package together.

I also believe games are ultimately experienced differently by every individual. Reviews, opinions, and spoilers can only say so much before someone actually sits down and experiences the game firsthand. In the end, each person becomes the protagonist of their own experience, and despite all its flaws, Scarlet Nexus ultimately gave me the experience I was personally looking for within it.

The first 10 hours or so was truly addicting, I'm getting to know a new world, getting used to all the fighting mechanics and following along with the characters' stories, I honestly couldn't put this game down. But the deeper I get into it, the more I realize how much of a wasted potential this turns out to be. 

An interesting premise that is butchered by terrible and mediocre writing. It looks like whoever wrote this story just goes on the internet, looks up all the most popular sci-fi tropes and stuff them all together without even realizing the mess they've made. There are numerous times during the story that I have found myself wondering if I have skipped over a few chapters or something, because nothing makes sense. Remember that interesting plot point that we introduced a few chapters ago and made a really big deal out of it? It's gone. You probably don't need to understand that anyways, or anything that's happening for that matter because we will soon introduce another completely unrelated, tropey and cheap plot twist to try and hook you on the story. Meanwhile, Yuito has the mental capacity of a toddler, even a tragedy happening right before his eyes is unable to sway or make him display any emotions that a normal human should have, and of course he's completely cool hanging out with his enemy right that afternoon for a cup of coffee because why not? People trying to kill him? No problem, but don't go insulting his favourite doll because then he will seriously get angry. At first, I was hyped to play both routes and understand the whole story from different perspectives, but now I don't even think that I will touch Kasane's route.

The combat is flashy and satisfying, I really love how different SAS enables different kind of gameplay approach to combat. The biggest problem is, however, instead of a smooth hack and slash experience, you will often time find yourself in situations where you are animation locked in a combo or action and unable to dodge the enemies' attack. Overtime, mobs and bosses become damage sponges that are very frustrating to play against, the mechanics themselves are simple, but it feels like you are just punching a wall over and over for 10+ minutes with no effects whatsoever. The upgrade system is also extremely unimaginative, instead of actual interesting perks, the abilities offered are getting up after being knocked down, double jump, doing an extra attack, or +5% damage etc.

I usually don't write reviews so this is more of just some of my thoughts scrambled together, but I feel like I have to write this review because I am so disappointed. I have read a lot of articles and reviews about how good this game is, and I decided to grab it while on sale. I was blown away during the first few chapters of the game, the art, combat and story are all promising to be a blast, but i guess it apparently didn't turn out that way. This game could have been something much more, something way better, but they took all of that potential and tossed it right in the trash.

Combat is fun, fast, better than I expected and easily the main reason I enjoyed this game.
Characters have a surprising amount of time dedicated to them and there are individual relationships to (optionally) explore, which lead to tangible in-combat bonuses which can change the way you play once you unlock them. I liked most of them well enough, but some are especially stereotypical.
Story is a bit stereotypical at times as well but not so much that I found it unenjoyable or particularly predictable, there are a few twists along the way and I didn't have any major issues with it.
On the technical side, the game ran very well for me (4K 120FPS almost all the time on a 2080 Ti) and I think the characters look good, but the environments and environmental textures aren't that great and a bit bland. Environments could've used more attention.
There are optional sidequests, but they're almost all "kill X monsters of type Y with method Z" and the "method" part is sometimes frustrating and unnecessarily time-consuming to set up. The sidequests are probably the weakest part, they basically exist as excuses to have some more fun with the combat.

Overall this isn't a masterpiece but it's a solid game which I recommend. If you like what you see you'll probably enjoy it.

This is the best looking anime game out as of right now by a mile, and it isn't even close. The visuals in 4k are absolutely beautiful.

No problems so far on 4k max settings, unlocked frame rate and no frame dips so far with an rtx 2080. A lot of JRPGs are poorly optimized and run like trash so this was a pleasant surprise. The story so far has a good mix of seriousness plus humor so i'm excited to see where it goes. They do visual novel style storytelling where the main story is mostly still images with two character models talking to each other. There are pretty interesting transitions with an comic book esque flair to it that keep it from getting boring. This style may not be for everyone, so i suggest you look up a video to see what i'm talking about if you're not familiar with it. 

The combat is very well done in my opinion, the integration of the main characters abilities into his combos is something i've never seen done this well in a JRPG. A lot of the people complaining about combat if you've noticed really havent gotten that far into the game. I don't understand how you can judge something as repetitive after only playing the tutorial. You can't dodge cancel out of combos which some people will think is clunky but if you don't just mash the attack button or play on easy you will be fine. The early monster's attacks are extremely telegraphed/ have kind of long wind up times so if they're having trouble dodging this should tell you a lot about their general skill level.  I also saw someone complain about getting stun locked, very early into the skill tree there's an ability that allows you to recover from down so there's that. 

Overall if you're a JRPG fan this is a easy day 1 pickup, please don't let the negative reviews deter you the production quality top notch and the gameplay is fun and engaging. If you're not the anime tropes and style of storytelling may not be for you so definitely do some more research before picking this game up.

I think some of these negative reviews hit it on the head. All-in-all, it's a mediocre game with a nice coat of paint on it. When I first saw this game's unveiling trailer, I was instantly drawn by its art style. I'm a big fan of games that utilize 2D-esque visuals such as games made by ArcSys, so naturally I was a big fan of Scarlet Nexus' graphics from the beginning. They're honestly some of the best, if not the best, anime styled visuals in any video game and I hope that future games utilize similar aesthetics.

Scarlet Nexus is overall a fun, action JRPG with a good combat system and competently in-depth skill tree. If you have ever played Astral Chain on the Nintendo Switch, this game shares many similarities with the latter and those who enjoyed Astral Chain will certainly enjoy Scarlet Nexus. What hurt this game's combat is that there's not enough enemy variety. Enemies you see in the beginning are ones you'll see throughout the game's entirety. Sure, they'll have variations, but there simply isn't a good amount of variety. 

There's a lot to like about this game. From its great visuals and music to its fun and quirky features like character bonding and gifting. The story imo was nothing amazing, as it was the run-of-the-mill JRPG filled with your typical anime tropes and ends with heroes beating the villain with the power of friendship. That being said, I enjoyed most of the characters and the game makes you care about them.

For me, the biggest flaw is that the game developers decided to cheap out on the cut scenes. As I mentioned above, they're reminiscent of something you would see in a visual novel and there's definitely a lot of talking and dialogue involved, which may bore players at first.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game. I'm glad I bought it and experienced it and for those who are hesitating to buy it, I would certainly recommend it. It's a shame that there's no demo on PC, however.

Gonna keep this review as spoiler free as possible, because I do think that some people will enjoy this game. After waffling back and forth on it, I finally settled on giving this a negative review. That said, this game *does* have some good things, and the actual gameplay itself is fun. Combat is fun, making use of multiple allies abilities is fun, the visual aesthetics are great, the music is awesome. The overall story itself is relatively predictable, but decent and I liked it.

However, those things make up a small fraction of the game. I've got two big gripes with the game. First and foremost: the actual *telling* of the story kinda just sucks. The big overall picture is fine, but when you zoom in on the small scale details - like the character interactions and decisions - a lot of it is just outright stupid and nonsensical. On top of that, characters will outright contradict themselves at different points in the story. For example, during one of the early chapters in the female PC story, you sorta arbitrarily decide you need to kill someone without giving much thought to it, and your allies go along with it begrudgingly, until you ultimately fail and they talk some sense into you. Then in a much later chapter (about 2/3 - 3/4 through the game), during a bond episode with an ally, the PC asks them what made that ally decide to kill someone they had killed prior, and then the PC says word for word "It's just......killing someone. Is it that easy for you to do? I don't understand how you could make that decision so easily, even if it is to achieve your goal. There's no way I could do that."
......
Yes, those exact words come out of the mouth of the PC that took nearly no time to decide to kill someone for their own goals much, much earlier in the story.

And second: it's really obvious that someone higher up saw the success of games like Persona, said "I want that, make it happen, I don't care how," and so that's what happened, and it just sucks. The game is split up into phases/chapters, and in between each you return to a hideout with your team, where you can socialize, give them gifts, and raise your "bond level" with them, and occasionally there will be "bond episodes" with them that are effectively copycats of the Persona hangouts, where you learn a bit about the character and deepen your relationship with them. It's executed *poorly*. It's awkward and completely out of place in this game, and it would've been really great if you could just ignore it, but remember that bit I mentioned about using your allies' abilities in battle? Well those improve SIGNIFICANTLY as you level up your bond with the respective ally, so it's more or less required. It got really, really exhausting every time I'd boot up the game after saving at the hideout to spend 30+ minutes just buying gifts, giving them to people, and watching these bond episodes when the entire process feels poorly made, sloppy, and like it doesn't belong in the game at all.

Also, there's side quests. Kind of. They aren't good, relevant, or rewarding. "Kill x enemy type y times with z method" and you get 2 medium healing items type quests. Feels very shoehorned in and forced.

This game feels like it had one or more higher ups with different creative directions, and rather than focusing on one identity to be, it tried to be a bit of all of it and stretched itself too thin on most of it, resulting in a lot of really lackluster mechanics, and writing that was poor and contradicted itself at times. The game would have been significantly better if they just did not do the character relationship mechanics at all, and were much more consistent on the character writing. The blueprints for a really great game are there - they just failed to put it together in a cohesive, well done way.

That said, I enjoyed the entire end segment starting from when you get to [spoiler]the tomb. [/spoiler] The rest of the game  from that point on was very good, and the rest of the game should have been like that. I'm overall disappointed with this game, but it wasn't all bad, and ending on a good note is definitely a plus. I just wish the rest was like it.

I loved it!  I found setting the difficulty to "easy" made the pacing and game overall much more enjoyable.  The story and characters were a lot of fun.  Personally I didn't love the bonding events as I felt they broke up the pacing but I just skipped through those.  Def recommend this game for any action JRPG/anime fan.

Really obviously made on a tight budget but they managed to get a good game out of it. While most of the story is told in slideshows as a trade-off, pretty much every non-npc line of dialogue in the game is voice-acted and very well, and there's a LOT of it too.  The story itself is alright, veers off into crazy 90s JRPG territory but that's kind of inevitable when you're trying to sell a high-concept story on a budget of 10 bucks and some gum. There's also two protagonists with entirely different stories & parties and they frequently cross over, adding heavily to replay value.

Also you get a neat base that slowly fills up with crap you gift your teammates(and they will start adding their own junk as you get closer with them) which is fun. Giving your gardening friend some plants, for example, ends up with flowers and vines all over the place. Give someone a booze set and bottles will show up in the kitchen. They'll also goof off with this stuff in their spare time, too. It's a nice bit of characterization on a budget. 

Gameplay itself is decent enough though somewhat hard to get used to, it's mostly about managing a suite of buff-like powers that alter your moveset in subtle or overt ways. Every action is very committal(for a character action game) and enemy damage is pretty high so you need to know your enemies' weaknesses and prioritize threats to effectively fight. Of course there's also a lot of items to help brute-force your way through so it's not TOO punishing on lower difficulties. 

Having different party members(and thus powers) most of the time means that both playable characters approach combat situations very differently too. Both characters do share a power in psychokinesis, which typically means weaving hurling junk at enemies into your combos but occasionally manifests in rad ways like surfing a bus through a crowd of enemies. Overall it's not super in-depth but it's good enough and doesn't overstay it's welcome.

Anyway it's not a life-changer or anything but it's a high-concept story told decently well on a budget and is an easy recommendation to buy if you like good ol' anime action games.

This game has two main protagonists, Kasane and Yuito. I have only played as Kasane.
 
The story was pretty well formulated but in my opinion it gets way too convoluted in the latter half. They keep throwing plot twists and surprises at you and the story just keeps getting more complicated. Maybe a good thing for some people but for me I think they should have dialed it back a bit. I only know the Kasane story but I’ve heard that the two story lines aren’t too different. Also they spoil each others story line so you kinda get a vague idea of what happens in the other character’s story.
Each side character has several bond episodes which are like side stories where your character and others hangout and deepen their friendship. I enjoyed most of them and doing them makes their powers stronger.
 
The gameplay/combat system was super fun. It revolved around their telekinesis power and something called SAS. I found flinging objects around to hit enemies enjoyable and some stages have special objects that do a lot of damage and have a unique animation. SAS is basically the other side characters sharing their power with you. So if you connect to the teleporting guy you can teleport and the same applies to any other character. A lot of enemies have special features where it was incredibly difficult to fight or attack them without a specific power.
There’s a skill tree that makes you stronger that I was able to get around 95% complete by the end. I only did a minuscule amount of grinding so just doing the main story should get around 80-90% of the tree unlocked.
One thing I gotta vent is that some of the stages are waaaay too tedious, especially the one leading up to the final boss. While clearing stages you encounter regular Others (“Others are what the enemies are called fyi) and then major Others which are kinda like mini bosses. The major ones aren’t particularly difficult but their health can take a bit of time to whittle down. So the problem is the final dungeon was absolutely littered with mini bosses and it got really irritating fighting like 30ish of them. I quickly ran out of those special objects and honestly I feel like I did something wrong because jeez it was way too time consuming to get to the final boss.

The art and animation were well done. You can switch the outfits of almost all the side characters and it also changes in all the cutscenes which is pretty cool. But I feel like they should have used their time and resources better because a lot of  the cutscene animations were cut short and they fell back on still images. Idk if there’s a direct connection between them but I personally would have preferred more animation time than being able to choose what they wear in the cinematics.

One of my favorite features was decorating the hideout and seeing the characters interact with their decor. Idk why I liked it so much but they kind of ruined it by making the drops to craft the decorations completely random. The only way to get some of the materials is to just keeping going to the same stage over and over until you get lucky so I didn’t finish some of the decor.

Honestly there’s somewhat similar games out there that are better but it was still a decent game and I don’t regret buying. $60 might be a bit too much for what it is though so I definitely recommend waiting for a sale if you wanna give the game a try.

I don't usually start the review with the game's mechanics but there are points to be made here and stories to be told so bear with me. Or don't. This thing will be wordy, anyways. Nexus is a hack and talk and slash action jRPG and as such, there are two obvious segments of game's loop to be discussed here.


[h3] .. There's blood on my hands, but I'm sure in the end I will prove I was right..* 
[/h3]

The crawling is a very solid base for the gameplay. There is everything here to provide a reliable 30+ (double that if you decide to finish the stories of both of the protagonists) hours of entertainment. There are numerous mechanics at hand and the game encourages - more accurately: enforces - mixing up the use of at least the few basic ones. I have encountered the reviews saying that, especially in the later parts of the game, the combat is tedious and repetitive and while I have enjoyed it till the very end, I cannot completely dismiss such opinions. Admittedly, some of the final dungeons are a bit lengthy. Furthermore, certain skills are locked behind leveling up both the protagonist and his (or her) relationships. That said, having maxed out my team, I've always had numerous options of interacting (and by interacting I obviously mean the merciless slaughter, since maxing out the relationships and picking certain skills makes the combat effortless on the default difficulty) with the antagonists. 

The dungeons are always linear with the objective clearly displayed and only the most basic puzzles scattered along the way. The enemies are not particularly varied either. 


[h3] ..is light and clear, petals in the wind.. * 
[/h3]

The second axis of gameplay is the standard visual noveling. During this phase, the protagonist talks with the team members, participates in bonding events that develop their relationships - and, as mentioned before, grant and enhance skills - crafts items and gives gifts. The crafting system is very basic and barely deserves a mention, still it is obligatory for creating gifts for the team, which makes it an important part of the game. 


[h3] ..is an extremely hard crystalized alumina, used as an abrasive. Hand in hand with sapphire.. * 
[/h3]  

The graphics are positively wonderful. And yes, I realize the fact that somewhere in the dark recesses of my nearly abandoned memories, lurk the times of graphic cards with the staggering 2 megs of vRam onboard and games running in 320x200px and (hopefully) about 20fps, so yes, I am perfectly aware of the fact that I might be impressed easily. And yet, behind how Scarlet Nexus uses the UE4, there is an idea. And ideas are bulletproof.

Take the general design. There is a heavily pronounced, almost comic-like distinction between the foregrounds and backgrounds. Most of the cutscenes are edited to resemble the static screens of a visual novel but rendered in a real time, so all the alterations to the looks of protagonists made by the player remain visible. And then those static screens smoothly transition into action when needed. 

Additionally, the locations look spectacular. The use of holographs for example. Most of the trees are holographic. So are the flags and banners, and the fireplace inside our base. There is a nightclub inside of which there is a holo-lake all over the floor, populated with virtual fish swarming around the protagonists' feet as they walk around.

Attention to detail is prevalent throughout every aspect of the game. The gifts that you offer your party members not only don't instantly disappear like in other games employing this particular mechanic, but the characters put them on the display in the team's hideout and are seen interacting with said items later. 

Music is more than OK. Does what it is supposed to. If the graphics in Scarlet are SS (on a scale from SSS to F) the music is a solid B+.     


[h3] .. of a brilliant red colour..* 
[/h3]
    
I've recently reviewed an uncannily similar story: telekinetic superhero kids, ancient conspiracies intertwined with teen drama slice of life. I've absolutely disdained the experience. It's all there, 2 reviews back. And yet I can't stop praising Scarlet. At first I thought it was because that last game was a visual novel. That the hours of hacking and slashing gave me the  needed relief from the walls of text. But no.                      

It's the protagonist all along. He is extremely optimistic - and not in an artificial or exaggerated way that jRPG characters are often guilty of. His optimism seems learned and trained, often extremely challenging to maintain in the face of events he faces. He is definitely not the one of the 'saint' type who apologize to every enemy they defeat and is not the one to heroically (and pathetically) sacrifice his life at the first mention of that being [strike]required[/strike] possible (I'm looking at you 'Tales of...' here), he is willing to explore the possibilities, to look past harms done to him even if he states it openly that he cannot forgive the guilty party. In short, he feels alive. And wildly likable.     

I realize that perhaps if I had chosen the other protagonist (both their stories and personalities differ significantly) my opinion of this game might have been less favorable. Still, while not as great as the lead, the other members of the party are a tremendously enjoyable bunch. Sure, most of them are stereotypical to the fault but the authors somehow take all those clichés and gracefully build on top of them. For example, the 'clumsy girl destroys a valuable piece of equipment' scenario. While other games play this to establish the character, here it is used to make the entire party cooperate in order to overcome the situation, which in turns tells us a little bit about everyone and even does that in a particularly elegant way.  
 
The story itself is the Fast and Furious of jRPGaming. It's an absolutely delightful concoction of mildly scientific fiction, traditional (but still engaging) teen drama and absolute, over the top, perfectly self-aware silliness that hits you when you least expect. Just take look at this (or don't since it's a mild spoiler from somewhere around one third of the story): [spoiler]The protagonists discover that their powers enable them to travel through time because it is not actually the telekinesis, but the manipulation of gravity that made them throw the objects around up to that point. It instantly made me think how - in a very limited, teen sci-fiction scope of narration - it made sense since all that gravity and mass folding the spacetime wibbly-wobbly stuff. And then, in that same sentence, without even blinking the eye, they mention how they're going to use it to launch the entire MOON two millennia into the past.[/spoiler]  I absolutely loved every second of it. 

And, quite surprisingly, there are times when Scarlet displays some ambitious depths and attempts at symbolism if you're patient enough to look for it. Eight plus out of ten, 7th place on my 2023 game of the year** list. When you look at it this way, you might have actually read this last paragraph to know my opinion instead of struggling through this entire, not particularly sober in retrospect, rambling. Tough luck.

I will preface this with the fact that I do like anime.  I don't watch a ton of it but I do catch at least one show per season, so I'm not coming at this game from a "weeb-hater" perspective, but to be frank, this game is everything that's bad about anime, in more ways that you might at first think.

But lets start with the positives.  As you may have noticed from trailers and other reviews, the combat is actually really good.  It starts off very simple, but as you gain more team members and tools at your disposal combat feels fluid and enemies are capable of threatening you, so there is a real seat-of-your-pants gameplay that is really enjoyable.  

Oh my mistake, I put a plural in positives.  That's it.  I can't really think of anything else truly enjoyable about this game, so lets talk about the negatives.

The [b]character's designs[/b] and personalities are cookie cutter anime stuff.  If you think "oh this character looks like x from x anime" you can pretty much guarantee that they will act like them too.  The cool out of touch beauty and the friend loving slightly dense male protagonists.  The lazy but actually super smart short girl, the big guy who actually has a sensitive side, the playboy with a dark secret, the nerd who can't catch a break, they are all there.  I won't even go into the big villain and his motivations because dear god are they trite as all hell.  

The [b]world and level design[/b] is pretty abysmal.  Not only are there relatively few environments, you will revisit all of them at least twice, if not 3 times.  At the start of the game I went to the same 3 areas twice each before finally being shown a cool new snowy mountain area.  AND THEN THEY MADE ME GO THROUGH IT BACKWARDS AGAIN.  And lets not even get me started about the final zone which is literally just a section from every single zone you've been in stretched out and connected end to end.  The town hubs feel like they are utterly empty, talking to people offers virtually no utility, and there are like 3 quests sprinkled through the city.  These things combined made me stop even visiting it unless i had to at all, instead choosing to just sit in my hideout between stages.  The actual levels are super linear but overly spacious.  You can always tell when there are stronger enemies coming up because all of a sudden there are a ton of throwable debris lying around and the formerly narrow corridor opens up into an atrium or something.  

The [b]story[/b] is as generic as walmart brand white bread.  There was exactly 1 twist that I didn't catch and that was because I couldn't be arsed to actually read all of the relationship conversation stuff with the playboy character.  There is a lot of deus ex machina, handwaving of atrocities, and plot holes.  I physically cringed when the female MC attempts to kill the male MC [i[THREE TIMES[/i] and everyone is like you should have just told us, its fine don't worry about it, we can still be friends (more on this in the relationship section coming up).  Same deal when the [Literal ending Spoiler read at your own risk] [spoiler]the final villain has a change of heart and sacrifices himself for the greater good.  And even more that he only was able to do so because the to MCs let him do the one thing that they had been trying to stop him from doing.[/spoiler].  This entire story wouldn't have happened if ANY of the characters had stopped and thought for a little bit. 

And now [b]relationships.[/b]  Oh god relationships.  So first let me explain how it works.  Between the "levels" you have the chance to return to your hideout with your current party and chat with them, go on mini events with them, and give them gifts.  As your relationship grows with them, so does your support system, which unlocks additional support powers and abilities,  So you'd think "Oh that's cool, so you have to choose which people you have to spend your time with and make trade offs as to which ones you want right?"  No, that would be GOOD game design.  And as we ascertained previously, this is BAD game design.  In this mode you can do it with everyone.  Give a gift to all up to 8 party members.  Go on dates with up to 8 party members, chat with up to 8 party members.  And why stop at one gift?  You can give 2, 3, or 4! As long as its something they like.  Or hell what not give them the exact same thing you gave them last time.  It has a similar effect!  Worse, all of these have tediously long cutscenes, with loading screens between them.   Which means that of the 18 or so hours of play time I have on file a solid 6-7 of them are me just mashing through cutscenes as someone confesses that they like someone else, or the big guy talks to me about cooking or gardening, or the shy girl says she doesn't blame me for trying to kill the person she likes or what ever.  Its ATROCIOUS.  And you do need to do them, to at least lvl 4 out of 6.  The power boost you get out of it is so significant that it makes some previously difficult fights far more manageable.   I hate it with a vengeance.  

[b]Enemy variety[/b] doesn't really exist.  There are like 4 or 5 main types of enemies, with 1 extra type per zone, and a couple of different riffs on the same ones.  For example "Pool" type enemies spit stuff at you from a range, but it could be oil, water, or electricity, or even fire depending on the zone.  But they all act the same and just apply a different type of debuff.  Initially in place of bossess they'll just stick a big healthbar on a stronger enemy and call it a day, but you do have the occasional good boss fight against an OTHER where it has some actual mechanics and you have to play with your various allies abilities to deal damage to it.  Other than OTHER bosses, there are two more types of boss fight, the x v 1 character fight and the x v x character fight.  The x v 1 character fights are pretty boring, because that 1 character will only have 2 main attacks, and then 1 rarer attack that they'll mix in there, and once you know the pattern its just a matter of throwing shit at them and stunning them until they die.  The X v X fights on the other had are a lot more interesting.  Since in these fights you'll be fighting the other protagonist and just like you they can use the abilities of their allies as long as they are alive.  So you might fight a guy with extra fire damage and high invulnerability, or fight him again with teleportation and stealth detection or something.  They are more fun because they will trigger two different phases based on how damaged they are that is actually hype as heck and looks very cool from a visual sense.  Shame their AI is absolute trash, making the actual fights trivial once you understand how they work.

[b]Miscellaneous other issues[/b] I hated how later in the game they just started throwing what used to be bosses but are now just stronger mobs at you in packs of 3 or 4 without actually balancing how they deal damage.  The few times I died it was because 2 or 3 of the large diving/beam enemies would juggle me with their beams while I'm focused on something else and I couldn't land and heal in time.  I really disliked how I couldn't get invested in any character because they are so generic and one note.  I was displeased with how empty the world was, and how large the levels were for how empty they were.   I hated how you only have one type of weapon and it just upgraded in a straight line.  I hated how upgrading your allies gear does nearly nothing.  I hated how you have 3 bits of equipment and you always have to run hp armor and damage, because all of the other ones are just worse. 

In conclusion, its clear this game was released far too early.  They maybe wanted additional levels, or to actually fill in the levels a bit more.  Or worse, I suspect that this was originally going to be an open world styled game and they ran out of funding.  The combat carries the game but its not enough to buy at $60.

At this price, I don't know yet.

Scarlet Nexus is a surprisingly good action-RPG. Gameplay wise it's very fast-paced, comparable to Platinum games and Devil May Cry. It's flashy, it's quick, and on higher difficulty will test your reflexes. It's not really open world: You can travel to large instances, be it dungeons or cities/hubs, using the world map. 

The story is set in a heavily sci-fi world, the cities colored with augmented reality advertisements and people messaging each other with just their brains. A setting where many people are born with psychic powers like pyrokinesis, teleportation, and invisibility. A world where nothing is as it seems, complex plots and conspiracies abound the corners of the underground. Reminds me a bit of Blade Runner. And you get to experience it from two different perspectives, in ENG or JP depending on your preferences. 

The journey is split between two characters, Yuito and Kisane. You can select who to start with, the other becoming another campaign option to play with on your next playthrough. Each campaign is around 20 hours worth of story, and while each of the two has the same superpower they have a different play style of applying it. Yuito uses a sword and is a melee rush-type, while Kisane is a ranged zoner with throwing knives. Selecting a character will not only lock you to that character's PoV, but also certain party members, though you will interact with the other team throughout the story and get to try to them out.

The gameplay's mostly set into "chapters", and you're allowed to rest between chapters in your hub area and interact with your party members, give them gifts, have "bond episodes" (think Persona's social links) with them to increase your relationship and in turn, make both you and them stronger. The characters can be a bit tropey at times, but they're not badly written, especially if you go through the bond episodes to flesh them out beyond the tropes. You can also visit other cities and talk to NPCs for world building and accepting side quests. 

Once a chapter start, it usually moves the story forward and takes you to a new area where combat is expected. The combat is VERY fun. Your character can attack either with their weapon or their superpower, telekinesis, in addition to the ability to "link" with 4 other party members and temporary gain their superpower as well. Your rotation often involves mixing your weapon attacks combos with your super powers, and using other people's superpowers, with other people's superpowers having 3 different ways of being used, allow for a large variety of combo and juggling potential. Once the combat "clicks", you'll be able to pull off some pretty cool combos.

Enemies are spread throughout the areas and you can engage them stealthily for extra damage (e.g. through teleportation / invisibility). There is no down time between battling and exploring, and you're able to escape or heal right away with the click of a button. In addition to difficulty settings ranging from very easy to very hard, should you happen to fall in combat there is a chance for your teammates to revive you, and you're able to revive them manually without items as well (though it takes time). The game can be as forgiving and as punishing as you want it to be, allowing both action rpg vets and newcomers to tailor their experiences. Personally I went with Very Hard and it was a pain but also really fun and rewarding.

Overall if any of this sounds good to you, I highly recommend getting this game. Esp if you like Action RPGs of this kind.

Scarlet Nexus, didn't have the slightest clue about the game, saw it on Steam when it released, deemed it nice, bought it.
Binged it really hard, took me about 50h to finish the game on both characters.All in all I had a blast, great fun. So, let's divide this review into a topics, shall we?

Overall design: 
-Scarlet Nexus is looking good, reminds me of a Cell shade and anime mixture. 
-Performance is solid. No crashes, twice some very minor lag. 
-Even though it says particial controller capability, it worked perfectly fine in every aspect. 
-The menus you have are pretty vast but well enough divided not to confuse. 
-Difficulties can be changed on the fly. 
-What I find very well thought out is the fact that in New game + (Ex new game as they say) you can replay with the other character and decide to keep your progress, or start anew. Once finished with two stories, you can freely switch. Well done.

Gameplay:
- Firstoff, the game has a lot of Visual novel esque Cutscenes. By that I mean: Fucktonns of Dialogue. Which I personally appreciate, but it might not be for everyone.

- Levels are usually, areas with diffirent subsections. Relatively straight forward in design, some optional areas with extra items. While progressing, certain areas will lock you in untill you killed all enemies. Depending on what enemies it spawns. That can become annoying. Though to be fair, it's still perfectly fine in my opinion. Theres a nice variety in design, you come across diffirent areas, mostly urban, but not repetetive in looks. The enemies that spawn depend on the character you're playing, reasons below.

- Combat is relatively simple. You have the same button layout for both characters, each one has their Unique fighting style however. Close range with Yuito, and Kasane with some wider midrange attacks. Where they come together is that both can or rather should chain their attacks into Psychokinesis follow up combos. Timign seems to be a bit odd sometimes, but hell does it look cool, prolonging and extending my ass kicking of the enemies. Additionally there is mechanics like the S.A.S where you can borrow powers from companion characters like Superspeed, electrokinesis and much more, which you will need to kill certain enemies in reasonable amounts of time. Additionally you can call those characters in for one attack. Other mechanics include a power up mode and the brainfield, where you go beserk basically.

- Each character has their own Skilltree too. The so called Brain Map. The contents are pretty similar, you have the same branches. Diffirences for example are that Kasame gets more air-combo attacks, while Yuito has the longer ground combo. Some of the same skills are placed at diffirent spots in the trees too. Some things are harder to obtain for one, or the other.
Here comes my first gripe. Some essentials like recovering from getting hit, or dashing mid air is something you need to skill, because otherwise the flow of the game is attrocious. Getting hit happens, taking 5 seconds to stand up is, annoying to say the least. Luckily, all those things can be skilled early on. And the skills overall feel all usefull.

-Sidequests.. were there, gave some more or less usefull stuff. On paper they were easy to do. You just have to kill some enemies, nothing else provided. However, you need to kill them specifically. And that is where I gave up on them, because the game did not tell you how it defines some things. For example. Psychokinesis finish. Whats that? Killing an enemy by throwing an object? Nope. First you need to skill it. Then you need to knock down the enemy onto the floor, then it will play an extra animation, which must kill the enemy. Nothing else counts. Which especially with harder enemies, and some types. Is..not worth the effort.

Enemies:
- The enemy library in this game is relatively long. Don't be fooled however it ismostly the same enemies, with diffirent "elements" Some are oil, some are water for example, which makes certain S.A.S skills more efficient against them, or which can give you a negative condition. Some of the more "Armored" enemies can become quite the sponges though and with some of their moves, they managed to rise my pulse admittedly. Still, nothing overly hard or gameplay worsening. I probably also sucked pretty hard at points. There are a few bossfights though they feel rather specifically designed and the AI really likes running away and beeing hard to hit. Once again, no major hassle. One last note, enemies drop items, which are used to purchase goods. The grind is kept relatively low however.

Characters: 
- The characters are for the majority divided by the character you choose, ending later on in the game. In the standby phase of each chapter, (aka breaks) you can have some dialogue, give them gifts and increase your bond level, which enhances their SAS abilities. Theres also bond episodes, in which heart felt conversations take place in the quest to understand each other better. (Apologies for the trace of sarcasm here)

The diffirent characters are all quite unique, have their own personailities and stories and during the course of the game there is some really well displayed character development and humor. The banter and talk they have is quite well written.
HOWEVER be warned. Those characters contain an immense level of anime tropes, stereotypes and the genereal disease of: "No I cannot tell you this for reasons, even though it would be logical because it would probably shorten the story by 50% if we talked like adults." Theres also a few very stupid or illogical choices. *cough BBEG, cough* (Sorry must 've been the cold weather)

World & Story:

- In sooth? The world is in a ll God Eater, or Code Vein fashion with bits of humanity beeing advanced, but diffirent governments, trouble and most of all monsters threatening them, so we need the super natural defense force. While it might not be the most unique overall setting, the Brain punk stuff is great and the world has a really intrieguing portrait too. Things throughout the story are well established and explained, it seems sensible enough and makes a good impression. I'll keep it vague here to avoid spoilers.

-Story itself is interesting. It is large diffirent, depending on which character you play, it intertwines and becomes more aligned later in the game, shared cutscenes exist. It is well made and kept me really hooked to find out more about the individuals. Sure, you could probably classify it as some teenager drama to some degree, which probably isn't a wrong way to see it. Fun nontheless.

Resumee:

- All in all I think Scarlet Nexus is a very good game. Gameplay feels good. Fighting feels fun and efficient, story is interesting and keeps one going, despite of the downsides. Difficulty is adustable and sometimes even on normal challening. If you can live with the very stereotypical tropes and anime storytelling, you're gonna have a blast. But I can very well understand if you do not aswell.

Personnal raiting, I'd give this game a solid, 8.5 Trying to see it more objectively, with all that it has, it's probably a solid 7, depending on prefference. I hope this was enjoyable / helpfull to read. Have a nice day.

- Don't bother with side quests

[b]Character Progression: (8/10)[/b]
- Has skill tree called Brain Map where you can spend points
- Yourself and 8 companions: Can equip 1 unique weapon, 3 unique plug-ins (ATK, DEF, HP boosts, etc), alternate costumes and 3 cosmetic accessories
- Weapon progress can only be upgraded to the next level available and so on
- No weapon variety
- Increase companion bonds (up to Level 6) by doing their "Bond Episodes" (more cut scenes), can also be increased by gifting items of their interest, and replying to brain messages
- Increasing companion bonds would result to increased SAS effects from different companions that you can activate at the same time even without having them equipped in your party which allows for many different synergies. Your heart won't melt or anything but you'll gain interesting character backstories, you will learn that other members still care for other members even though they are now enemies, you will learn that this chick is the daughter of this family and her aunt is a deceased girlfriend of this "main villain" at the time, you'll also learn that the silent/shy clairvoyant chick can actually see through how big your "organs" are, so on

[b]Combat: (9/10)[/b]
- Combat opens up after [b]7 hrs[/b] 
- Has lock-on, can enable auto lock-on to whichever you are currently attacking
- Basic 3 hit combo, 1 AOE attack and dodge,  succeeding combo strings can be learned via brain map
- Dodging will limited at first, will feel clunky with no animation cancel, not a lot of iframes, this is because you'll get a companion around 7+ hrs in I think who has a teleport skill. Upon activating a companion skill, you are 100% iframed, then dodge teleport > deactivate the skill again > continue the combo
- The basic string would 3 hit combo + 1 AOE > To Telekinesis > To rush back in > To 3 hit combo > To Aerial > To 3 hit Combo + AOE > To another Telekinesis while in the air
- In between, you'll be activating 1 or multiple Companion abilities at a given time depending on the situation. You can activate invulnerability+poise to continue to stringing your combo, you can activate teleportation to clutch a dodge, you can activate weapon effects like fire/electricity, you activate duplication so your combo string hits 3 times every single hit
- The depth of the combat is with the companion SAS combination and activation in-between your basic combo which greatly makes up for the lack of weapon variety and moves
- Think DMC light meets Genshin Impact but with having 4 other party members without the tedious swapping of characters and having all 4 special effects on at the same time
- [i][b]Edit: Companion abilities have 2 types, passive effects and active skills for each. It really opens up around 15-18 hours once you have all 9 companions including Kasane and can equip 8. From the 8 equipped, you can activate 4 passive skill effects at the same time (i.e electric/fire sword+duplication (3)+slowdown time+teleportation), on top of that you can string any of the equipped active skills seamlessly to your own combo[/b][/i]
- Brain Drive basically is just an automatic gauge that automatically fills up and activates which enhances combat efficiency
- While Brain Drive state is active, Brain Field can be used, which is just a super of sorts
[i][b]Edit: By the end of it, random characters would show up and increase your Brain Field timer before it runs out which could effectively go on almost infinitely until the encounter is done[/b][/i]

[b]Difficulty: (9/10)[/b]
- Highly suggest doing Hard (nothing Harder than Hard)
- Difficulty scaling is good, no one-shotting of any sort here but you can still die if not careful
- Will constantly be using healing potions, party heal items or reviving companions
- Will be pressed to utilize all companion skills on every situation specially boss fights

[b]Encountered Glitches and Bugs: (9/10)[/b]
- 1 crash in 11+ hours
- Encountered numerous crashes after 1.02, resolved by completely removing MSI afterburner

[b]Fun: (9/10)[/b]
- Anime, check
- Waifus, check
- Combat and Story will really open up after a few hours, if you refunded in less than 2 hours, you are definitely missing out
- Not every new game release needs to be genre defining, mind blowing game mechanics, deep big-brain story and be over 100 hours of play to have any perceived value
- I would personally give it plus points for trying different things, new enough to keep it fresh
- [i][b]Combat is exceedingly fun at the later half to the end game juggling all 8 companion passive and active skills[/b][/i]

[b] Total: 8/10 [/b]

Scarlet Nexus gives a bad first impression. Your move-set is very limited in the first few hours of the game. However, if you stick with the game, it will open up and get much better the farther in you get.

The first thing I would want new players to know is that the dodge sucks and you should not go into this game expecting the dodge to work like most other action games. Scarlet Nexus doesn't have a standard "block" button, so you might assume you are intended to primarily dodge enemies attacks. There is even a "perfect dodge" mechanic (similar to other action games like Bayonetta's "witch time" mechanic) that will entice you, but you will quickly find that the dodge just isn't reliable. Whether the dodge being unreliable was intended by the developers or not, Scarlet Nexus is actually better that the dodge is not reliable, because dodging would be overpowered if it was reliable as perfect dodging provides a ton of invincibility frames. Instead of perfect dodges, you need to focus on understanding enemy attacks and positioning yourself outside of hit-boxes. You will also unlock an ability that grants temporary invincibility on a cool-down and that should be your go-to method of defense if you cannot avoid a hit-box. TLDR: don't rely on the dodge; Scarlet Nexus isn't that kind of game.

The second thing I would want new players to know is that Scarlet Nexus has numerous settings that I would recommend changing such as 1 setting the camera distance to "far", 2 setting SAS activation animation to "off", 3 setting camera motion blur to "off", 4 setting brain crush animation to "short", and 5 setting difficulty to "Very Hard" (more on difficulty in next paragraph). So don't hesitate to check the settings menu; there are even more settings I change from the default, but those are the most important in my opinion.

There are multiple difficulty options and you can change the difficulty setting at any time from the settings menu. I have been playing on "Very Hard", which is the highest difficulty currently available for me to select, and I have enjoyed playing the game at this difficulty. I occasionally die to mob fights, and I tend to die several times to each boss fight. Although I would recommend playing on "Very Hard" if you are experience at playing other action games, there are some enemies that are absolute bullet sponges with WAY TO MUCH HEALTH! Specifically the large "others" boss fights are the main bullet sponge offenders, and their fights are just painful for how long they can last, so I wouldn't knock anyone for turning down the difficulty for the specific boss fights I have in mind. Usually Action JRPGs are way too easy, but Scarlet Nexus is no push over and will give you a decent challenge which I really appreciate.

Luckily all cut-scenes and dialogue scenes are skip-able. I found myself skipping multiple of the dialogue sections in the early sections of the game, but as the game has progressed I stopped skipping the cut-scenes because I am actually enjoying the story. I think the story is quite good, and the voice acting is top notch. Everything you would want to be voice acted is voice acted. Also the cut-scenes are not pre-rendered, so your skins will show in the cut-scenes.

I really like all the characters in Scarlet Nexus. It is so common for animes and JRPGs to have annoying, whiny characters, but Scarlet Nexus doesn't fall prey to that trope. Most of the characters in Scarlet Nexus exude confidence and it is so nice to see it.  

The game has an auto-save feature that saves very frequently, so you should never lose any considerable progress. If you die you are given the option to retry the current fight. You can also manually save at the frequent save spots. There are multiple save slots per game.

One of my major complaints is the controls for items. You cycle through items with the left/right buttons of the directional pad and press down on the direction pad to use an item. These controls are just really clunky for how fast paced the game is, and it is really hard to distinguish one item from another. For example there are about a dozen different healing items: light jelly, medium jelly, all light jelly, all medium jelly, etc. and all these healing items are the same green color with nearly identical icons. Expect to use the wrong item on accident a lot.

Although this is marketed-as/considered an "RPG" the progression systems are pretty straight forward. Your character levels up automatically as you gain experience. As you level up you will gain points you can spend in the skill tree (which the game calls the "brain map"). You can occasionally talk to your NPC allies to increase your "bond level" which will upgrade your "SAS" abilities. You can change your equipment, but equipment very simple with just a weapon and a handful of passive boosters. Overall, the progression systems are very simple and quick, which is good; the game will keep your focus on what is important, playing the game, not being stuck in menus.

The game has a very good file size. Despite the developer requirements listing a necessary 50GB of space, the game is currently using <20GB for me and I have created multiple saves. Most modern games are making no effort to reduce file sized, so I very much appreciate Scarlet Nexus for doing so.

Overall, very happy with this game. :)

The game's story definitely isn't the best that's out there. If we want to compare them to TV anime, this would probably rate about a 5-6/10. Decent, but not great, as it's interesting enough to keep you entertained on a regular day but doesn't exactly make you jump out of your chair in excitement when a twist happens.

However, this is not an anime, but a video game, and it is absolutely worthwhile to play this for its gameplay value. The best way to describe this game is that it's basically Force Unleashed on steroids had an illicit lovechild with Persona. Oh, and Metal Gear Rising is the lovechild's favorite uncle. It has everything Force Unleashed has with regards to the "Force" powers available, you can use the abilities of your companions in a similar way as you would in Persona, essentially making the MC the wild card who is able to use all personas (read: psionic abilities) in the game, and has all the high octane, fast pace combat that you get from MGRR.

The best part about this is for all the things that you can do, for all the things that happen on-screen, not once have I felt like the game became a janky mess or things happen that don't make any sense, something I actually can't say for either Force Unleashed or MGRR, which is a significant consideration given the fact that this game was made by a smaller company than either of the other two. The best part about it is the plethora of abilities you have don't always guarantee victory, wherein a combination of skills work best against certain enemies/environments.

tl;dr, this game's greatest value is in its gameplay, which is really the biggest thing you could ask for in a game in general. So if your dream game is one where you're an anime Jedi with Naruto powers, this is it right here.

One of the things that a lot of people give reasons of recommending Scarlet Nexus is because of its great fluid combat. You start of with just mashing attack over and over to at some point strategies just click in your head. Of course you should use invisibility to go behind enemies, of course you should use fire after splashing oil on your enemies. This strategic dance comes to me with hours of playing and testing but once it clicks and a strategy comes it feels really great.... or you can just mash the buttons until something dies.

But I want to give reasons why the story/writing might be Scarlet Nexus's strongest tool and is the hook for me to play and reach 100% achievement. The story and the gameplay are intrinsically intertwined, there's a reason why you have the powers you have the way it is and the fact that Bandai Namco are able to weave it beautifully and make me invested in the story was something I felt was worthy of applaud. My power level was increasing on par with my investment in the characters story.

The game is literally the power of friendship - the game. Even the final villain's objective is to push their own version of the power of friendship or what they are willing to fight for their friends... and the kicker is that the antagonist actually won, and the execution was great. I had to give props to the writers for being able to pull that final part off. Yeah there are a lot of cringe moments. the female mc is always brooding and sometimes you wish you can shout at her to just grow up, and the male mc is a goody two shoes, but as the story goes their characters become more mature and develop more. Its a good simple story in my opinion. 

The writers knew the themes they wanted to push, they write and weave it in the best way they can with a great gameplay and the ending was great if there is some foreshadowing for some unknown sequel and they respected your intellect and didn't pull some unknown crazy stunt. Worldbuilding was spot on and felt lived in, everything that existed had a purpose and didn't just felt like it was there just to look cool, it all served a purpose. One gripe however was the Kodama mystery which I thought was a miss opportunity. 

The last part I wanna give props is to the way they do new game plus. There are two separate characters line but they both eventually converge in the end. I thought this was brilliant. By the time I've finished playing the male mcs story, I felt the story was already good and finish. Any other player that was strict on time I believe can finish there and get their money's worth imo. Doing the second mcs story is just to tie loose ends and to get more game from the combat. I think they executed this really well. One of the benefits I thought that having two mcs with two branching story paths with the finale coming together was that I notice the mc didn't fall into the calamity of the mc syndrome where it felt like the world revolved around them. In essence whilst playing one of the mcs there is always that idea in the back of my mind that other events are happening, this made the world felt more lived in as well as  allowing for different perspective of the mc when playing each of the story. I personally wish Bandai Namco can try out other games with this style of new game plus.

In conclusion, Scarlet Nexus is an underrated game and you should really give it a try, at least for the great gameplay.

It took me ~42 hrs to beat the game once on one out of two story tracks (Kasane), with no backtracking to previous areas or grinding more than necessary, almost no sidequests and missions, and being sure to do every single Bond (friendship level path) with each party member. Considering this adds up to a total of over 80 hours potential game time across both story paths, that's content on the level of the best Tales games, which is really impressive!

I originally thought this game was a bit too linear and lacking in depth, but what it really lacked was breadth -- there's no traversable world map, for instance. No shopkeepers aside from the single one that comes with each save point, which are very regular occurrences. However, this also lends to a streamlined experience that takes the time to get into its great cast of characters, and the Bond system directly correlates to increased capability with the battle system.

Battles are what this game lives and dies on. It's a very unique action RPG system marrying familiar elements (attack, dodge, jump) with new ones—right-click throws objects from the environment, G uses special objects (like dropping oil barrels on an enemy to drench them in flammable oil and make them vulnerable to Pyrokinesis), and of course, the SAS system. SAS is how you use the unique psionic powers of the different characters on your main character. Use Electrokinesis to empower basic attacks and make them stun, or Duplication to multiply thrown objects for more damage and shell breaking potential.

It's a very fun, challenging, and most of all extremely satisfying system to play with. It's so viscerally beautiful to execute staggered enemies with cutscene finishers after bringing them down with team attacks.

Now, should you get this game on sale or not? Personally, I purchased it on sale. Honestly, though, given the wealth of content available between two full story paths that explain the mysteries of the other, different difficulty levels, and new game plus with the new missions & challenges, I would actually say yes, this game is well worth full price!

Ignore my playtime on here as I played and finished this game on the PS5. As of writing this, I have finished Yuito's story and started my second playthrough already with over 46 hours clocked in. 

I'll just give the rating first and it is a good 8.5/10. I do recommend it. Be sure to read my last two paragraphs if you choose to stop here after the rating. 

The combat is great and fluid with a lot of interesting ideas and combos but with a few small issues. 
- Locking on can sometimes be wonky as in the character refuses to attack in the direction of the enemy I locked on to or simply locking on to the wrong enemy, This messes with the flow of combat severely and can definitely ruin some moments in game that requires fast reaction. 
- The combos and attacks are great and varied but required a long time to get and even longer to get the power combos. In fact, the best part and most fun you can get from the combat only comes after 20 hours due to them requiring skill points to unlock movement skills and bond points to unlock powers. All this is fine if not for the super tedious amount of grinding needed to get all the movement skills and powers. In short, you will most likely only be able to experience the best the game can offer near the end game and by then it's been a long journey of sub-par combat. 
- Unfortunately, there are not much weapon varieties. In fact there are basically none for better or worst. The characters you choose are strictly one playstyle of weapon which is different between the two main protagonist. Yuito uses swords while Kanase uses throwing knifes. Both are restricted to those weapons and that's it. Any weapon you purchases from the shop are only straight up bigger numbers to damage and a cosmetic change, nothing more. Now this isn't 100% terrible because while it does kinda suck to be force to play with one weapon the whole game, the benefit of doing this by game design is that these weapons are very fleshed out. There are so many movement skills and power skills that can be mixed together to create some truly fun combat. 

The maps and locations in game are decent. It's what you can expect from Bandai style anime games with linear maps and forces you to go in one direction and maybe a few rooms with little bonuses if you choose to go there. 
- The aesthetic of the game in general is pretty good and the locations are mostly good as well. Just don't expect anything mind blowing or amazing but nothing bad or terrible either. 
- The locations are obviously based off Japan but there are also a lot of European inspired locations as well. 

For the soundtrack and music, it's absolutely great. While not on the level of Nier Automata, it's doesn't need to be to still be good music. It's good enough that I went and bought the Vinyl record for the game. 

Now the main reason I mostly buy these type of games in the first place is the story, weird I know but i'm the type of guy who watches porn for the plot.  But this time I have to say that the story is pretty terrible and disappointing. 
- Yuito is a terrible character. He's a goodie-two-shoes but to the extreme. To summerize, take your typical 2011 style wholesome anime MC tripe and make it worst. Bad things happen but he downright ignores it and sometimes acts non-human. 
- Kanase is the better of the two mcs. I won't say much more than that.
- The plot itself is probably the worst offender here. It has to be one of the most contrived plots I've seen in anime in recent years. It's safe to say it's downright terrible with little to no redeeming factors. It's literally one plot twist after the other and I've actually lost track of how much plot twist there were. The pacing is also terrible because you would be bomb shelled by one huge plot twist only to immediately and I say that as in THE VERY NEXT SENTENCE be bomb shelled by an even larger plot twist that ain't related to the previous plot twist. 
- That's another thing, the story is a contest on who can have a bigger plot twist but the opponent is itself. It constantly tries to outdo itself with nonsensical plot twist and horrible directions which is a shame because if you just stood with one and kept it that way then everything would be kinda fine. It's even worst when everything started off really good too but just slipped off a mountain and continued to roll downhill at increasing speeds. 
- It's also funny when you think about it because if you took out 90% of the plot twist, the ending would've still make sense and probably for the better too. There were just so many things that didn't need to of happened but for some reason it did and some of them don't even have a conclusion meaning it literally happened for the sake of it happened rather than progressing the story or plot. Some of it are literally ignored and never brought back or even fully explained.

But even with all these negatives, I still gave it a high score and a recommendation because it's just simple fun. The negatives while horrible, doesn't really take away the fun factor of this game which is the gameplay. For me, if the story is absolute ass but the gameplay holds up then I can give it a free pass but that's just me. 

Though for those who value story, character, and plot more then I wouldn't recommend this title at all especially to those who can get very angry at nonsensical stories and characters with a lack of common sense. For those on the edge, I recommend you wait for a discount or sale of at least 30%-50% percent. Only buy this at full price if you've seen some other reviews and gameplays and still want to get it. Other than that, thanks for reading!
